records.our_prose: Parsley (Petroselinum crispum) is a hardy biennial herb in the carrot family (Apiaceae), grown for its flavorful, vitamin-rich leaves. Its biology is the mirror image of warm-season herbs like basil and the opposite of fast cool-season herbs like cilantro. Parsley is COOL-TOLERANT and FROST-HARDY, taking light freezes and overwintering in mild zones, yet it is also genuinely HEAT-TOLERANT: because it is a biennial that does not flower until its second year, it does NOT bolt from first-year summer heat the way cilantro does, so a single planting yields leaves spring through fall, and only the most extreme desert and subtropical summers slow it. That long, flexible season is the headline. The signature challenge is at the start: parsley seed germinates slowly and erratically, often 2 to 5 weeks, so growers soak it and wait. It is harvested cut-and-come-again from the OUTER stems, leaving the center to regrow for months. It comes in flat-leaf (Italian) types, with the stronger, sweeter flavor cooks prefer, and curly (French) types grown for garnish, plus Hamburg root parsley grown for an edible root. The one catch is the biennial cycle: an overwintered plant bolts in its second spring and the leaves turn bitter, so parsley is sown fresh each year for the best leaves. Pests are few, chiefly the parsleyworm (the handsome black swallowtail caterpillar, often left for the butterflies) and aphids, and disease is minimal.

records.our_prose: Your parsley came up thin, very late, or not at all. Parsley seed is slow by nature, often 2 to 5 weeks, and germinates poorly in cold, wet soil or when the surface dries out. Next time, soak the seed in warm water for up to a day, keep the surface moist, use fresh seed, and simply wait longer before giving up.

records.our_prose: Parsley is a light to moderate feeder grown for steady leafy growth over a long season. The University of Minnesota suggests a 5-10-5 fertilizer at about 3 ounces per 10 feet of row, once or twice during the season, on top of compost worked in before planting. Because you cut from the same plants for months, a light midseason side-dress of nitrogen keeps fresh green leaves coming; in containers a dilute liquid feed every 3 to 4 weeks replaces what frequent watering leaches out. Avoid heavy nitrogen, which draws aphids and softens the flavor.
records.source_context: Fertilize plants in garden beds once or twice during the growing season, using a 5-10-5 commercial fertilizer at a rate of three ounces per 10 feet of row. Use a liquid fertilizer at one-half the label recommended strength every three to four weeks for container-grown plants outside and every four to six weeks for parsley grown indoors.

records.our_prose: Parsley is one of USU Extension's named Table 1 crops: St. George's Group B (Semi-Hardy) planting date is about March 1. The seed is notably slow, taking 2 to 5 weeks to germinate, and leaves are ready roughly 80 days after sowing, from late May. Parsley is more heat-tolerant than its cool-season herb neighbors and does not bolt in its first year, so the stand holds through June even as St. George's summer heat, which routinely reaches 100°F in July per USU Extension's Washington County frost and elevation data, slows growth and toughens the leaves. A second direct sowing in early August, timed a little ahead of the quicker herbs to give this slower crop enough runway, follows USU's general fall-gardening guidance for restarting cool-season crops (Fall Gardening in the St. George Area); the fall stand is ready from mid-to-late October and, thanks to parsley's own frost tolerance down to about 10°F, carries a slow cut-and-come-again harvest on past the average November 1 first frost and right through winter, into late February ahead of the next spring sowing.

records.our_prose: Parsley can be direct-sown or started indoors. Its seed germinates slowly and erratically, often 2 to 5 weeks, and germinates poorly in cold soil, so soaking the dry seed in warm water for up to 24 hours before sowing speeds and evens emergence. Direct-sow about 0.25 inch deep as soon as the soil can be worked in spring, since parsley tolerates frost. To get a head start, sow indoors 6 to 8 weeks before the last frost and transplant out after hardening off; parsley moves better when young, before the taproot is long, so transplant on the early side. Keep the seedbed evenly moist through the long germination.
